| [NOTE-339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-339.md) v2 | Examining the Society of Mind | An exposition, read in full. Singh dates the Society of Mind to Minsky and Papert's early-1970s robot work, finds its agent in the procedure-bearing frame of 1974, and quotes the unpublished 1976 book drafts. He sorts the 1986 book's mechanisms into agents, simplest agents, agency construction, problem solving, communication and growth. Agents need no shared code: K-lines, randomly wired buses and paranomes stand in for messages. He finds near-relatives in Bayes nets, case-based reasoning, blackboards, Cyc and Soar, and concludes that the theory has never been implemented. Its claims of lineage are asserted, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self" | A hypothesis essay. A Self is the set of parts that pursue goals together, and its boundary is the farthest region of space and time it can measure and act on, its "cognitive light cone". Selves grow from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks, and cells form larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions. Every level that has its own goal is a Self, so living systems hold many nested Selves at once; the paper says this against IIT in one bracket. It has no model, no measurement of the light cone and no new data, and it confines claims about experience to a closing speculation. | Read |
| [NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md) | The Emotion Machine | Read in the 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think: each emotional state is a selection of mental resources turned on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem, and ordinary thinking uses the same switching. On this design sit six levels of mental activity, panalogies that link descriptions across realms, and a Self that is a network of partial models. It is argued by example and analogy, with no experiment and few neural claims. Against Damasio, the body is a resource the brain exploits, not what an emotion is made of; on Elliot it proposes, without evidence, the reverse causal direction. | Read |
| [NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md) | Intelligence without representation | A methodological manifesto with working robots behind it. Brooks argues that AI should build complete autonomous Creatures incrementally and test them in the real world, and that intelligence should be decomposed into parallel activity-producing layers, each running from sensing to action, not into perception, central reasoning and action. His robots have no central representation or control, and their coherence exists "in the eye of an observer", as in Minsky's account of human behaviour. The evidence is three layers on one robot, described, not measured, and the broad hypothesis about representation is flagged as a hypothesis. | Read |
| [NOTE-429](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-429.md) | The Emerging Field of Emotion Regulation: An Integrative Review | Gross's founding review. Emotions are modulable response tendencies. | [NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda's action-readiness theory applied to impulsive action. Automatic appraisal of concern pertinence elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change a self–object relation, with control precedence. Emotions differ by mode of action readiness. Events draw several appraisals at once, and the resulting states of readiness interact, so impulse control and much emotion regulation are themselves emotional. Purposive impulsive action is grounded neurally in anticipating an action's sensory effects (PPC, premotor, cerebellum), with frontostriatal circuits for stopping. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. Will is the recursive bundling of choices by treating each as a precedent, which gives an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma and makes Kavka's toxin rational to drink. The same recursion predicts legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control, and premature satiation of appetite limits what will can do for emotional reward. | Read |
| [NOTE-445](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-445.md) | The Diffusion Decision Model: Theory and Data for Two-Choice Decision Tasks | The full diffusion model (drift v with across-trial SD η, boundaries 0 and a, starting point z with range s_z, non-decision time Ter with range s_t) fitted by the χ² quantile method. | [NOTE-446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-446.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | The paper proposes that dACC estimates the expected value of control: probability-weighted payoff of a control signal minus an intrinsic cost rising with its intensity. dACC uses that estimate to specify the identity and intensity of the control signal, which lPFC and subcortical structures (STN, LC) implement. The account unifies conflict monitoring, reward and prediction-error responses, effort costs and the override of defaults. | [NOTE-449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-449.md) | The Time Course of Perceptual Choice: The Leaky, Competing Accumulator Model | The LCA: dx_i = [ρ_i − k x_i − β Σ_{j≠i} x_j] dt/τ + ξ_i √(dt/τ), with x_i floored at 0. | [NOTE-452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-452.md) | The Intimate Contest for Self-Command | Schelling's essay proposes "egonomics", the art of managing oneself. | [NOTE-453](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-453.md) | Evolution of the Internal Family Systems Model | Schwartz's short statement of the IFS model. | [NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md) | Sophisticated Inference | Expected free energy evaluated recursively over the beliefs an agent would hold after each plausible outcome turns active inference into a pruned tree search over belief states, formally analogous to Bellman recursion. | [NOTE-461](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-461.md) | The Physics of Optimal Decision Making: A Formal Analysis of Models of Performance in Two-Alternative Forced-Choice Tasks | Proves the pure DDM is the continuum limit of the SPRT and so the optimal two-choice decider. | [NOTE-462](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-462.md) | An Accumulator Model for Spontaneous Neural Activity Prior to Self-Initiated Movement | A three-parameter leaky stochastic accumulator, δx = (I − kx)Δt + cξ√Δt, fitted to Libet-task waiting times (k = 0.5, I = 0.11, threshold at the 80th percentile of output), reproduces the readiness potential (r² = 0.96) and the linear mean–SD relation of waiting times (r = 0.9). | [NOTE-466](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-466.md) | HDDM: Hierarchical Bayesian Estimation of the Drift-Diffusion Model in Python | HDDM fits the full DDM (v, a, z, t with sv, st, sz) by MCMC in PyMC, with group-level priors such as μ_a ~ Gamma(1.5, 0.75), μ_v ~ N(2, 3), z_j ~ invlogit(N(μ_z, σ_z²)), and the Navarro–Fuss likelihood. | [NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md) | The Haken–Kelso–Bunz (HKB) model: from matter to movement to mind | Kelso's retrospective on HKB. The relative-phase equation dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ has stable in-phase and anti-phase states for b/a > 1/4 and only in-phase below; with noise the switch is a nonequilibrium phase transition with critical fluctuations and slowing. Symmetry breaking gives metastability (relative coordination); merged with Kuramoto it models groups. The same dynamics is reported within and between people and in brain activity. A first-person account, not a review. | Read |
| [NOTE-826](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-826.md) | Turvey — Preliminaries to a theory of action | An essay, not a study. The executive cannot command muscles one by one, so acts are built from relatively autonomous coordinative structures, reflexes and their functional combinations, a term Turvey takes from Easton (1972). Higher levels specify equivalence classes of acceptable states and tune the parameters of these units, like the stiffness and rest length of a spring. The spinal cord is shown, by reflex probes, to be retuned before a voluntary movement, and optical information may set the tuning directly. | Read |
| [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md) | Ashby — Design for a Brain | Adaptation is the stability of the organism–environment system in the region where the essential variables stay within limits. To find such stability in an unknown environment, a second feedback must change the parameters of the first whenever an essential variable leaves its limits: the ultrastable system, shown in the Homeostat. Its blind search takes time exponential in the number of variables unless partial adaptations are kept, and keeping them needs a system that is not fully joined, its parts separated by constancies. New learning destroys old to the degree that it uses the same parts. | Read |
| [NOTE-954](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-954.md) | Powers, Clark & McFarland — General Feedback Theory, Part I | Builds a hierarchy of negative-feedback control systems in which each order perceives only the feedback signals of the order below and acts only by setting their references, which are replayed recordings of their own past perceptions. An "imagination connection" sends those references back into the higher system's perception, so that it can remember, plan "mentally", hallucinate and dream, under a "mixing control" the authors cannot specify ("We are open to suggestions", p. 20). An inherited N-system, driven by error in intrinsic physiological variables, reorganizes the network at random, forming new input functions as well as new outputs; an organization persists when the behaviour it produces lessens intrinsic error. | Read |
| [NOTE-959](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-959.md) | Powers, Clark & McFarland — General Feedback Theory, Part II | Names six orders of perception, from spinal loops through sensations, configurations, sequences and relationships to system concepts, with demonstrations whose reaction times lengthen with order (about 0.3 s at third order, 0.4–0.45 s at fourth). The N-system "merely alters the properties of a system, thus changing the transformations applied to existing information" (p. 37): reorganization is a change of perception, felt as insight, and a new perceptual organization can be vetoed by imagining its use. Consciousness is defined as a feedback function under N-system action. Conflict freezes a lower system at a virtual reference, and a system switched "entirely to the imagination-connection" is one of the ego's defences. | Read |
| [NOTE-963](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-963.md) | Powers — Feedback: Beyond Behaviorism | A control system "will produce whatever output is required in order to achieve a constant sensed result" (p. 77), so behaviour is the control of input, not output, and stimulus-response laws follow from the environment once the controlled quantity is found. Above the lowest level a system's output is a reference level for the level below, so the hierarchy closes through lower systems down to muscle effort sensed kinesthetically; its top is a set of inherited intrinsic reference levels whose error drives reorganization. The paper says nothing about imagination: every loop it describes closes through the environment. | Read |
| [NOTE-1102](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1102.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | A commentary. Control theory adds to goal talk the need to perceive the present state and compare it with the goal. Psychopathology arises where the loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are sensitivities to classes of goals. Valence tracks the velocity of goal attainment against a reference value, so approach and avoidance can each produce either sign. Confidence, doubt and disengagement lie outside the loop, in expectancy-value theory. | Read |
| [NOTE-1111](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1111.md) | Hesp et al. — Deeply felt affect: the emergence of valence in deep active inference | A computational proof of principle with no data. Valence is a state of self, inferred at a slower, deeper level from affective charge, the update to the expected precision γ that sets how far the preference- driven action model, rather than habit, governs policy selection. Positive charge is rising confidence in the action model and negative charge falling confidence. The valence level sends priors on γ back down. "Felt" means explicitly represented, which the authors take as necessary, not sufficient, for self-reportable valence. For the record, this is the closest existing model of that felt valence is the system modelling its own potential. But its sign and intensity run against the record's potential account for negative valence, and it inherits the wanting/liking problem. | Read |
| [NOTE-1124](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1124.md) | Gollwitzer & Sheeran — Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis | A meta-analysis of 94 tests (1990–2003, 8,461 participants, mostly students and laboratory tasks) finds that adding an if-then plan to a goal intention raised goal attainment by d = .65 against the goal intention alone, across four problems of goal striving, with large effects on cue accessibility and on the immediacy, efficiency and non-conscious running of the planned response in small sets of tests (k = 1 to 7). | [NOTE-1131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1131.md) v2 | Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer — The when and how of planning: 642 tests of implementation intentions | A meta-analysis of 642 tests (294 reports to September 2019). Forming implementation intentions improved behaviour (d = .27), cognitive performance (.47), affect regulation (.66) and social judgement (.52), pooled d = .36; publication bias was substantial, and a robust Bayesian estimate is d = .15, small and highly heterogeneous. Contingent if-then plans beat schedule plans (.43 against .29); rehearsing the plan once helped, recording it hurt, and effects were large only when motivation was high. | [NOTE-1424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1424.md) | Haken, Kelso & Bunz — A theoretical model of phase transitions in human hand movements | A theory paper. | [NOTE-1433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1433.md) | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner — Critical fluctuations | As bimanual wrist or finger movement is paced faster, the standard deviation of relative phase grows as the anti-phase pattern nears its switch to in-phase, peaks in the transition (about 85° mean phase, near the 90° of a uniform spread), and falls once in-phase is reached; started in-phase, the same movement shows neither a switch nor that growth. | [NOTE-1449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1449.md) | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner — Dynamics governs switching | Four people switched on cue between in-phase and anti-phase finger movement. Going from in-phase to anti-phase took about twice as long as the reverse at every frequency tested, with a longer-tailed distribution, significant for each subject. A stochastic HKB equation with the earlier experiments' parameters plus a term pulling relative phase toward the intended pattern reproduces the asymmetry and the shapes, with one parameter set to the right order of magnitude: the less stable a pattern, the faster it is left.
